Prioritise team goals or OKRs by picking pairs

A planning meeting with twelve candidate objectives usually ends with eight of them "top priority". Choosing between two goals at a time forces the trade-off the meeting avoided, and the team's order falls out of everyone's answers.

The starter list

Question: "Which goal matters more this quarter?"

  1. Cut churn
  2. Launch in a new market
  3. Ship the self-serve plan
  4. Reduce support backlog
  5. Hire two engineers
  6. Improve onboarding
  7. Raise prices
  8. Pay down tech debt
  9. Win three enterprise deals
  10. Improve site speed
  11. Start a partner programme
  12. Get SOC 2 ready

Why picking pairs works here

  • Each person answers alone before the meeting, so the plan starts from everyone's view rather than the first person to speak.
  • The team table shows each goal's 90% rank range two ways: for these people, and for the wider group they stand for. A goal whose range runs from 2nd to 10th is one the team has not agreed on yet.
  • The agreement score (0 to 1) and each goal's best-to-worst place across people show whether you have one plan or two camps.

What it doesn't do: It ranks what people think matters, not what is feasible. Size the work separately, and put hard commitments (a contract, a legal deadline) outside the list rather than letting a vote rank them.

Compared with what you'd use today

Dot voting on a whiteboard, a shared spreadsheet with 1 to 5 scores, or a paid planning tool. Scores cluster at the top and dot votes follow whoever goes first; pairwise picks give a full order and show the disagreement instead of averaging it away.

Under the hood: a Bradley-Terry model refit after every answer, an adaptive question picker, and a stop rule checked against simulated respondents, including ones whose picks are close calls. The method and its measurements.
